analysis.one_liner: Gives donors a federal tax credit for giving to nonprofits that pay private school tuition for children.
analysis.headline: The House Ways and Means Committee approved the bill 23–16 in September 2024 and placed it on the Union Calendar, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let taxpayers subtract donations to K-12 scholarship charities directly from the federal taxes they owe — a credit of up to $5,000 a year, capped nationally at $5 billion per year from 2025 through 2028. The charities would award scholarships to students from households earning up to 300% of their area's median income, usable for private or religious school tuition, tutoring, therapies, and homeschool materials. The bill died in the House without ever getting a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Families who want to send their children to private or religious schools, or pay for tutoring, therapies, or homeschooling, would gain a new funding source through scholarships from nonprofit scholarship organizations. Higher-income taxpayers gain the most directly: the credit is a dollar-for-dollar reduction in federal taxes owed, worth up to $5,000 a year or 10% of income, so donors who can afford large gifts capture the biggest share of the $5 billion annual cap.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Private school families and scholarship nonprofits

how_it_helps.text: It gives families a new funding stream for private school tuition, tutoring, therapies for children with disabilities, exam fees, and homeschool materials, provided household income is at or below 300% of area median income.

Scholarships themselves would be tax-free to the student's family, and the bill forbids governments from controlling scholarship organizations or excluding private and religious schools from receiving the funds.

It carries accountability rules for scholarship organizations: income verification, annual independent audits, a bar on self-dealing, and a requirement to distribute essentially all receipts as scholarships.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on federal taxpayers, who would effectively fund the scholarships by giving up up to $20 billion in tax revenue over four years (2025–2028) with no offset, meaning either higher deficits or other taxes. Because credits are allocated first-come, first-serve, the largest tax reductions would go to the highest-income donors able to give early and in bulk. Public schools could also lose enrollment and the per-pupil funding tied to it as families leave for private schools.

drawbacks.text: Donors would receive a dollar-for-dollar federal credit worth up to 10% of their income or $5,000, so a wealthy donor could redirect up to $5,000 in taxes they owe to scholarships of their choosing — a credit worth more to high earners than the deduction it replaces would be.
The $5 billion annual volume cap is allocated first-come, first-serve, so donors and organizations best positioned to file earliest capture the credit first.

The bill bars any government control over scholarship organizations or private and religious schools receiving the funds, and prohibits states from excluding religious schools, limiting public oversight of publicly subsidized spending.

The roughly $20 billion in credits over four years reduces federal revenue with no stated offset, and by subsidizing exits from public schools could shrink funding and enrollment for the systems most lower-income children remain in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill contains real taxpayer safeguards — audits, income verification, anti-self-dealing rules, a mandatory 90% distribution of receipts, and a hard four-year sunset on the credit — which is more design discipline than many school-choice tax bills have. But its central mechanism is a large, hard-to-audit transfer: donations channel through intermediaries to private schools with federal dollars, the first-come-first-serve cap favors wealthy early filers, and the funding is not offset. It would strengthen private and religious schools at the expense of the federal treasury and, indirectly, public school budgets, while delivering tuition help mainly to families already able to pay most of private school tuition.

outcome.mechanism: The Ways and Means Committee passed it on a party-line vote and put it on the House calendar, but party leaders never brought it up for a vote before the term expired, so it died.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 6, 2024 and referred to the Ways and Means and Education and Workforce Committees.
On September 11, 2024, the Ways and Means Committee approved it 23–16, with Republicans in favor and Democrats opposed.
It was reported to the House and placed on the Union Calendar on October 4, 2024, but no floor vote ever occurred.
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No federal money was diverted from the treasury or from public school enrollment through the new credit. Taxpayers avoided a roughly $20 billion four-year cost, and the private school scholarship industry did not gain its new federal funding channel.

sides.party_line_note: The 23–16 committee vote split cleanly on party lines, with all Republicans in favor and all Democrats opposed; the bill had only Republican cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill creates a federally subsidized tuition stream for private and religious schools and bars governments from excluding them based on religious character or policies. The bill also locks in the private-scholarship industry's role by defining scholarship granting organizations as the permanent channel for the public money.

New organizations administering these scholarships would handle up to $5 billion a year in tax-credited donations, with a guaranteed revenue stream and statutory limits on government control over how they operate.

Subsidized exits to private schools would draw students and the per-pupil funding attached to them away from public systems, though the effect depends on how many families use it. This concern was raised by opponents of the bill.
